title: WSD learning-rate schedules
summary: Why warmup-stable-decay replaced cosine for many LLM runs: how a long constant-LR phase plus a short cooldown matches cosine, why the loss plunges in the decay, and how it makes scaling studies cheap.
outcomes: Explain why cosine decay ties the learning-rate curve to a training length chosen in advance
Write down the WSD schedule and compute its LR at any step for linear and 1-sqrt cooldowns
Explain the sharp loss drop in the decay using the river valley picture
Choose cooldown length, shape and floor using published ablations
Plan a scaling study with one constant-LR run per model size and branched cooldowns

lessons.title: Why cosine forces you to fix the training length up front

blocks.md: In the prerequisite course you met warmup followed by **cosine decay**. For large language models (LLMs) it has been the default since GPT, and large models such as Gopher and LLaMA used it too. After warmup, the learning rate (LR) typically decays to 10% of its peak. Hägele et al. (2024) call it the de-facto standard schedule.

blocks.caption: Cosine decay to 10% of the peak (warmup omitted). T is the cycle length: the step where the LR reaches its floor. After T the LR stays at the floor.

blocks.md: The catch is the single parameter $T$. The Chinchilla paper (Hoffmann et al., 2022) found that the best loss for a given number of training steps $S$ is reached only when $T$ matches $S$, and that overshooting $S$ by more than 25% clearly hurts. MiniCPM (Hu et al., 2024) reproduced this on a 0.036B-parameter model: for runs of 20 to 80 tokens per parameter (20N to 80N tokens for N parameters), the lowest loss always came from $T = S$; both $T < S$ and $T > S$ were worse.

blocks.title: Cosine to 10% with cycle length T, run stops at step S

scenes.caption: T = S: the LR reaches its 10% floor exactly when training ends. At the halfway point it is still 0.55 of peak, at 0.9 S it is 0.122.
T = 0.6 S: the LR hits the floor at 0.6 S and then crawls at 10% for the last 40% of training. Too little time at high LR.
T = 1.4 S: when training stops the LR is still well above the floor, so the run never fully anneals. Chinchilla saw clear damage beyond 25% overshoot.

blocks.title: Toy model: final loss above the floor of 2.0, by cycle length

scenes.caption: Computed with the simplified toy model from lesson 3, not a real LLM, 10,000 steps. T = S wins (0.554). Ending too early costs 0.020, overshooting by 40% costs 0.032, and never decaying (constant LR) costs 0.197.

blocks.md:
This coupling causes three practical problems:

1. **Mid-run checkpoints are underestimates.** Halfway through a cosine run the LR is still 55% of peak, so the checkpoint is worse than a model that was trained, and annealed, for that many tokens.
2. **Extending a run is awkward.** If more compute arrives after $T$, the LR is already at the floor, where progress is slow. Rewarming it causes loss spikes that recover slowly (Hägele et al.).
3. **Scaling studies get expensive.** To learn how loss depends on data size, you need a separate run from scratch for every length.

blocks.prompt: Chinchilla's Approach 1 trained each model size (70M to 10B parameters) with four different cosine cycle lengths. If a study uses m model sizes and m data sizes, roughly how many training runs does it need with cosine?
blocks.reveal: About $m^2$: one run from scratch for every (model size, data size) pair, because each data size needs its own $T$. MiniCPM describes the cost as $O(m^2)C$ for an average per-run cost $C$. The rest of this course shows how a schedule that does not depend on $T$ brings this down to about $m$ long runs plus cheap short branches.

blocks.md: Cosine couples the **shape** of the LR curve to the **end date** of training. You must choose the training length before you start, and every checkpoint before the end is half-annealed.

blocks.question: A teammate evaluates the 50% checkpoint of a cosine run (T = S) and concludes that 'training on half the data gives loss X'. Why is X misleading?
options: The checkpoint has seen only half the data, so X is accurate by definition
The LR at that point is still about 0.55 of peak, so the model has not been annealed; a run with T equal to half the length would reach a lower loss
Cosine checkpoints are always better than fully trained models of the same length, so X is too optimistic
Weight decay has not taken effect yet at 50% of training
blocks.explain: Mid-run cosine checkpoints are underestimates. Most of the loss drop from annealing happens when the LR gets small, which for this run only happens near S. A cosine run with T set to the shorter length would anneal earlier and end lower.

blocks.question: You planned 100k steps with cosine (T = 100k), but the cluster time is cut and you must stop at 70k. Which outcome is most likely, compared with a run planned for 70k from the start?
options: Identical loss: the schedule only matters at the end
Lower loss, because the LR stayed high for longer
Higher loss, because at 70k the LR is still well above the floor and the run never annealed
blocks.explain: Stopping at 0.7 T is equivalent to a cycle that overshoots the stop by about 43%, the regime where Chinchilla reports clear degradation. The model has not had its low-LR phase.

lessons.title: Warmup, stable, decay: the schedule and its loss curve

blocks.md: MiniCPM (Hu et al., 2024) split training explicitly into a high-LR part and a decay part and named the result the **Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD)** schedule. Warmup ramps the LR up to the peak $\eta$ over $W$ steps. The **stable** stage holds the LR constant at $\eta$ until step $T$. The **decay** stage (also called the **cooldown** or annealing phase) lowers it with a decreasing function $f$ until the final step $S$.

blocks.tex: \mathrm{WSD}(s)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{s}{W}\,\eta & s<W\\[4pt] \eta & W\le s<T\\[4pt] f(s-T)\,\eta & T\le s\le S\end{cases}\qquad 0<f\le 1\ \text{decreasing}
blocks.caption: The WSD schedule as defined by MiniCPM. Note that T now marks the end of the stable stage, not a cosine cycle length.

blocks.md: Hägele et al. (2024) studied the same shape under the name **constant LR + cooldown**, noting it had earlier been called a trapezoidal schedule (Zhai et al., 2022). The cooldown usually takes the LR to zero, mirroring the warmup. The key property: until the decay starts, the schedule does not depend on when training will end.

blocks.title: WSD with a cooldown of fraction F of training

scenes.caption: Cosine (grey) starts decaying right after warmup. WSD with linear cooldown over the last 20% holds the peak until 0.8 S, then falls straight to 0.
F = 0.1, the MiniCPM default: the LR stays at peak for 90% of training. Its area under the curve is 0.95 of the peak times S, versus 0.55 for cosine to 10%.
The 1-sqrt cooldown of Hägele et al. drops faster at first and lingers near zero longer. Halfway through the cooldown it is at 0.29 of peak, versus 0.5 for linear.

blocks.prompt: Two runs share the same peak LR and length. Run A uses cosine (T = S); run B uses WSD with a 10% cooldown. At 80% of training, run B has clearly higher loss than run A. Which run do you expect to end lower?
blocks.reveal: Neither wins by much, and B often edges ahead. MiniCPM reports that once the decay starts the loss drops sharply and quickly reaches a level equal to or lower than cosine at $T = S$. Hägele et al. found an almost perfect match between the best cosine and the best cooldown runs across lengths. The high loss during the stable stage hides progress that only the decay reveals.

blocks.title: Toy model: loss above 2.0 during training (10,000 steps)

scenes.caption: Step 2,000. Cosine has already started to lower its LR and is slightly ahead (0.822 vs 0.839). The three high-LR runs are identical so far.
Step 5,000: cosine is at half its peak LR and leads by 0.100. A plot of these curves would make WSD look like the worse schedule.
Step 9,000: WSD-20% has been decaying for 1,000 steps and already dropped from 0.756 to 0.636. Cosine, at 0.562, is still ahead.
Step 9,500: WSD-10% starts its decay at 9,000 and falls from 0.756 to 0.638 in 500 steps.
Step 10,000: WSD-20% ends at 0.538 and WSD-10% at 0.550, both below cosine (0.554). Constant LR never anneals (0.750). Simplified: the toy exaggerates sharpness; real gaps are small.

blocks.md: Because the stable stage is independent of the end date, you can **branch**. Save checkpoints along the stable stage. To get a finished model at any length, start a short cooldown from the nearest checkpoint. To train longer, resume the stable stage from the latest pre-decay checkpoint at the same peak LR. MiniCPM verified that continuing the stable stage and then decaying again reaches the same loss as a cosine run planned for the longer length.

blocks.title: One stable run, many finished models

scenes.caption: Warmup, then a single stable run at constant LR. Checkpoints are saved along the way; nothing about the run depends on a planned end.
A cooldown of about 10% of each model's total length is branched from each checkpoint. Each branch is a short side run; the main run keeps going at the peak LR.
Need a longer model later? Resume from the last stable checkpoint, not from a decayed model, so the LR never has to be rewarmed.

blocks.md: Hugging Face Transformers ships this schedule as `get_wsd_schedule`. It takes the warmup, decay and either the stable or total step counts, a `decay_type` of `"linear"`, `"cosine"` (the default) or `"1-sqrt"`, and a `min_lr_ratio` floor that defaults to 0.

blocks.title: The WSD multiplier from Transformers, simplified to linear warmup

scenes.caption: Step 50 is in warmup: the factor is 50 / 100 = 0.5. With a peak LR of 3e-4 the optimizer uses 1.5e-4.
Step 400 is in the stable stage (100 to 799): factor 1.0, LR 3e-4. This branch does not depend on the total length at all.
Step 850: decay progress p = 50 / 200 = 0.25. The 1-sqrt shape gives 1 - 0.5 = 0.5, so the LR is already halved a quarter of the way into the cooldown.
Step 950: p = 0.75, f = 1 - sqrt(0.75) = 0.134, LR 4.02e-5. Linear would still be at 0.25.
Step 1000 and beyond: the function returns the floor, min_lr_ratio = 0.

blocks.question: You run WSD and save a checkpoint every 5k steps. At 60k steps you decide to train to 100k. Which checkpoint should you continue from?
options: The latest stable-stage checkpoint (60k), continuing at the same constant peak LR
The end of the 6k-step cooldown branch, rewarming the LR to peak
A fresh run from scratch with cosine and T = 100k
blocks.explain: The stable stage is the reusable trunk. Continuing it at the same LR needs no rewarm and later gets its own cooldown. (A variant that resumes from the decayed model, WSD-S, appears in lesson 5, but plain WSD rolls back to the pre-decay checkpoint.)

lessons.title: Why the loss plunges during the decay: the river valley picture

blocks.md: Why would a run that looks worse for 90% of training catch up in the last 10%? Wen et al. (2024) propose that the pretraining loss looks like a **river valley**: a deep gorge with steep hillsides and a river winding along the bottom. Any loss value splits into a **river** component (how far along the valley you are) and a **hill** component (how high up the walls you are).

Stochastic gradients make the parameters bounce between the steep walls. With a high LR, the bouncing is large, so the hill component is high, but each step also moves further along the river. With a low LR, the iterate sits near the bottom but crawls along it. Their conclusion: keep the LR high as long as possible to make river progress, then decay quickly to stop the bouncing and reveal that progress.

blocks.caption: The toy model used in this course (our own, simplified). u is LR / peak. The river term shrinks with S, the area under the LR curve. H is the expected excess loss of noisy gradient descent on one steep quadratic direction.

blocks.md: Where does the $H$ update come from? On a quadratic wall with curvature $h$, a noisy step is $y \leftarrow (1-\eta h)\,y + \eta\,\xi$, where $\xi$ is gradient noise. Squaring and averaging gives the update above, with $\eta_{peak} h = 0.02$. Its steady state is $H^* = 0.01u/(0.04 - 0.0004u)$: 0.2525 at the peak, 0.1256 at half the peak, 0.0250 at a tenth. **The hill height is roughly proportional to the LR.**

blocks.title: Watching the hill component settle as the LR drops
blocks.code:
H = 0.2525    # hill loss at peak LR (u = 1), steady state

def run(u, steps):
    global H
    for _ in range(steps):
        H = (1 - 0.02 * u) ** 2 * H + 0.01 * u * u

run(0.5, 25)   # halve the LR
run(0.5, 75)
run(0.1, 500)  # drop to 10% of peak
run(0.0, 100)  # LR = 0

scenes.caption: At constant peak LR the bouncing is in steady state: H = 0.2525. The stable stage never gets below this, which is why its loss curve looks flat.
Halve the LR. After 25 steps H has fallen to 0.2024: each step shrinks H by the factor 0.99^2 and adds less new noise.
After 100 steps at half LR, H = 0.1426, approaching the new steady state 0.1256. The drop is fast because the walls are steep.
At 10% of peak the shrink factor per step is only 0.998^2, so settling is slow: 500 steps bring H to 0.0409, still above its steady state 0.0250.
At LR 0 nothing moves: H stays 0.0409. A decay that is too abrupt freezes whatever bouncing is left.

blocks.md: A lower LR does not remove the hill instantly: the walls only pull the iterate down while it still takes steps of reasonable size. That is why the cooldown needs a minimum length. MiniCPM found a 2.5% decay falls short where 10% suffices.

blocks.title: Toy model at step 10,000: where the loss comes from

scenes.caption: Constant LR: the most river progress (0.498, area 1.0 x S) but the full hill (0.253).
Cosine (T = S): the hill is almost gone (0.026), but its area is only about 0.55 x S, so the river part is the worst, 0.528.
WSD, 10% decay: river 0.501 (area about 0.95 x S) and hill 0.050. Total 0.550, slightly below cosine's 0.554.
WSD, 20% decay: a little river progress traded for a lower hill (0.035). Total 0.538, the best of the four.

blocks.md: Real runs show the same signatures. MiniCPM tracked gradients in the decay of a 0.2B model: the gradient norm shrinks, successive gradients mostly point the same way (positive cosine), and the estimated curvature along the path grows by an order of magnitude, consistent with settling into a minimum. Hägele et al. linearly interpolated the weights between a checkpoint before and after cooldown and found the loss falls smoothly along that line, as if the model slides into one connected basin.

Tissue et al. (2024) fit full loss curves with an empirical law in the same spirit. $S_1$ is the area under the LR curve (river progress) and $S_2$ is an **annealing area** that accumulates LR decreases with a momentum factor $\lambda$ of 0.99 to 0.999. Fit on a constant and a cosine run, it predicted loss curves of unseen schedules, and it explains why cosine works best with $T = S$: shorter $T$ loses area, longer $T$ loses annealing.

blocks.caption: Scaling law with LR annealing (Tissue et al.). L0, A, C and alpha are fitted per setup.

blocks.question: In the river valley picture, why is the loss during the stable stage a bad indicator of how good the model will be after cooldown?
options: Because the validation set changes between stages
Because the high LR keeps the hill component elevated, hiding river progress that the decay will reveal
Because the stable stage only learns embeddings
Because the loss is computed with dropout on during the stable stage
blocks.explain: Loss = river + hill. A high LR inflates the hill part through bouncing between steep walls, so the plateau mostly reflects noise level, not lack of progress. The decay removes the hill part and the accumulated river progress shows up.

blocks.question: Using the toy numbers, a colleague proposes a 'cooldown' that drops the LR from peak straight to 0 in a single step at the end. What happens to the loss?
options: It falls to the river part, the best possible result
It explodes, because the LR changed too fast
It barely changes: with LR 0 no steps are taken, so the hill part stays where it was
blocks.explain: The hill only shrinks while the optimizer keeps taking steps at a moderate LR. With an instant drop to zero, H stays at its peak-LR value of about 0.25. This is the extreme case of a too-short cooldown.

lessons.title: Tuning the cooldown: length, shape, floor and data

blocks.md: **Length.** MiniCPM decayed from stable checkpoints at 40, 60 and 80 tokens per parameter (40N, 60N, 80N) and found that a decay of 10% of total tokens gave the best results, while 2.5% fell short. Hägele et al. found the benefit of a longer cooldown plateaus at around 20% and that the cooldown beats cosine somewhere between 10% and 20%. Wen et al. saw final losses match tightly for decay fractions from 8% to 12%.

blocks.title: Toy model: final loss above 2.0 vs cooldown fraction

scenes.caption: Linear cooldown. 1% and 2.5% leave bouncing behind (0.649, 0.598). Cosine at T = S scores 0.554, matched at about 10% (0.550). Gains flatten from 20% to 50% (0.538 to 0.535).
1-sqrt cooldown, same budget. It is better at every fraction up to 30%, for example 0.539 vs 0.550 at 10%, because it gets the LR low early and spends longer letting the hill settle.

blocks.md: Hägele et al. add an important nuance: the fraction needed shrinks for long runs, as long as the cooldown is long enough in absolute steps. On a 200k-step run, a 10k-step (5%) 1-sqrt cooldown almost perfectly matched cosine.
**Shape.** Hägele et al. tested several decay functions and found that **1-sqrt** consistently beats linear, with the gap growing for longer runs. With $p$ the fraction of the cooldown completed:

blocks.caption: At p = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 the 1-sqrt factor is 0.5, 0.293, 0.134; linear gives 0.75, 0.5, 0.25. The average LR over the cooldown is 1/3 for 1-sqrt and 1/2 for linear.

blocks.md: **Floor.** Hägele et al. kept the cosine baseline at the common 10% floor and found that decaying cosine lower improves loss to match the best 1-sqrt cooldown. They also saw that annealing all the way to zero can hurt some downstream benchmarks, and recommend sweeping the peak and final LR independently. Chinchilla, by contrast, found 10x decay slightly better than decay to 0 in its setup. Treat the floor as a knob to tune, not a constant.

blocks.title: LR / peak in each tenth of training, three production-style schedules

scenes.caption: Cosine to 10%, sampled at the midpoint of each tenth: 0.951 already in the second tenth, 0.48 by the sixth, and under 0.25 for the last three tenths.
DeepSeek LLM multi-step: peak until 80% of tokens, then 31.6% of peak, then 10% after 90%. Since 0.316 is 10 to the power -0.5, the two steps are equal on a log scale.
WSD with a 10% linear cooldown to 0 (MiniCPM-style length): peak for nine tenths, then a ramp whose midpoint is 0.5.

blocks.md: **Other decay forms in practice.** DeepSeek LLM used the multi-step schedule above (warmup of 2000 steps, then 80% / 10% / 10% stages) and reported final performance essentially matching cosine while letting the first stage be reused for continual training. MiniCPM-2.4B used exponential annealing, $f = 0.5^{(s-T)/T_h}$ with a half-life $T_h$ of 5000 steps (about 20B tokens at its 3.93M-token batch), after about 1T tokens of stable training at a peak LR of 0.01.

**Data.** The cooldown is also a natural point to change the data mixture. MiniCPM mixed high-quality and supervised fine-tuning data into the pretraining data only during the decay stage, and found this beat decaying on pretraining data alone. Hägele et al. note that Llama 3 used annealing on specific data to assess data quality.

blocks.question: Your WSD run uses a 2% linear cooldown, and the final model is noticeably worse than a cosine baseline of the same length. What is the most likely fix?
options: Raise the peak LR so the stable stage makes more progress
Skip the cooldown and use the last stable checkpoint
Switch the cooldown to an LR increase
Lengthen the cooldown to roughly 10 to 20% of training, or at least enough absolute steps
blocks.explain: A very short cooldown leaves the hill component frozen in place (MiniCPM: 2.5% falls short, 10% enough; Hägele: gains plateau near 20%). A higher peak LR would only raise the hill further.

blocks.question: Why can 1-sqrt beat linear for the same cooldown length?
options: It reaches low LR earlier in the cooldown, giving more steps for the bouncing to settle, at the cost of a little river progress
It keeps the LR near peak for longer during the cooldown
It never reaches zero, so the model keeps learning
It is identical to cosine to 10%
blocks.explain: Halfway through the cooldown 1-sqrt is at 0.293 of peak versus 0.5 for linear. Its average LR over the cooldown is 1/3 versus 1/2, so it gives up some area (river progress) in exchange for more time at small LR to shrink the hill part.

lessons.title: Cheap scaling studies, continual training and failure modes

blocks.md: The biggest payoff of WSD is for **scaling-law** experiments. Hägele et al. replicate a small study: model sizes from 33M to 360M, each at 10, 20 and 30 tokens per parameter. With cosine, each model is trained three times from scratch. With a cooldown schedule, each model is trained once at constant LR, and three cooldowns (20% of each length, linear) are branched from it. The cooldown runs scaled as reliably as cosine.

blocks.title: Training cost for three data sizes of one model

scenes.caption: Cosine: three independent runs of 10, 20 and 30 tokens per parameter, each with T matched to its length. Total cost: 10 + 20 + 30 = 60 units.
WSD: one stable trunk to 24 (80% of the longest), plus 20% cooldowns branched at 8, 16 and 24. Total: 24 + 2 + 4 + 6 = 36 units, 0.6x the cosine cost.
Add a fourth size, 40 tokens per parameter. Cosine needs a new 40-unit run (total 100). WSD extends the trunk from 24 to 32 and adds an 8-unit cooldown: 16 more (total 52).

blocks.md: Scaled up, the savings grow with the number of lengths per model. Hägele et al. estimate that the Chinchilla model suite, under their assumed setup of four token ratios (10 to 25 tokens per parameter) per model, would cost $5.59\times10^{23}$ FLOPs with cosine, against $2.36\times10^{23}$ with one run per size plus 10% cooldowns, about 2.4x fewer. MiniCPM used this trick to fit $L(N, D)$ from 6 model sizes (0.04B to 2B) with 6 decays each, and in their setup found a compute-optimal ratio of about 192 tokens per parameter, far above Chinchilla's roughly 20.

**Continual training.** Continuing from a pre-decay checkpoint at the same LR avoids the rewarming spikes that hurt cosine. Wen et al. go further with **WSD-S**: resume the trunk directly from the *decayed* checkpoint at the high LR, so the decay phases are not thrown away. On 0.1B to 1.2B models with 50B, 100B and 200B token budgets, WSD-S beat WSD and cyclic cosine, and matched cosine runs tuned separately for each budget.

blocks.title: WSD vs WSD-S when you keep training

scenes.caption: Plain WSD: the 50B model branches off, and continued training rolls back to the last stable checkpoint. The work done during the decay is discarded.
WSD-S: continue straight from the decayed 50B model at the high LR. Only one checkpoint needs to be kept or released, and the decay's river progress is reused.

blocks.md: WSD is **not fully schedule-free**. Optimal peak LR still shifts with training length: Bergsma et al. (2025) quote Shen et al. puzzling that the best WSD LRs differ by token count, and Hägele et al. found the best cooldown peak LR was about half the best cosine peak. Tune the peak LR at roughly the length you care about.

Other failure modes and limits reported in the sources:

- **If the length is known, linear decay to zero can win.** Bergsma et al. found linear decay-to-zero (D2Z) beat WSD by about 0.84% in loss for a 610M model at 80 tokens per parameter, though WSD beat linear decay to 10%.
- **Do not start a cooldown right after a loss spike.** Wen et al. saw validation loss worse by 0.02 when the decay began just after a spike; roll back a little or wait for the loss to recover.
- **Keep the pre-decay state.** Plain WSD continuation needs the stable checkpoint with its optimizer state, not just the released model.
- **Averaging is a partial substitute.** Weight averaging (SWA) on a constant LR closes much, but not all, of the gap to a real cooldown (Hägele et al.).

WSD separates *making progress* (long constant-LR trunk) from *cashing it in* (short cooldown). That separation is what makes checkpoints reusable, runs extendable and scaling studies roughly linear in the number of model sizes instead of quadratic.

blocks.question: You must produce models at 4 data sizes for each of 5 model sizes. Which plan uses WSD correctly to minimize compute?
options: 20 runs from scratch, each with WSD and a 10% cooldown
1 run of the largest model, with cooldowns used to simulate the smaller models
5 cosine runs with T equal to the longest length, evaluated at 4 intermediate checkpoints
5 long constant-LR runs (one per size), each with 4 cooldown branches from checkpoints
blocks.explain: Cooldowns replace the data axis, not the model axis: each model size still needs its own trunk. The cosine-checkpoint option is the classic mistake, since mid-run cosine checkpoints are not annealed and underestimate those lengths.

blocks.question: Your team knows the exact token budget for a one-off production run and will never extend it. Which statement best matches the evidence?
options: With a known budget, a well-tuned decay over the whole run (for example linear to zero) can match or slightly beat WSD; WSD's main advantage is flexibility
WSD is strictly required, because cosine cannot reach the same loss
WSD is always at least 10% better in loss
Any schedule is fine as long as there is warmup
blocks.explain: Hägele et al. found cooldowns roughly match tuned cosine, and Bergsma et al. found linear decay-to-zero about 0.84% better than WSD at 80 tokens per parameter. WSD shines when the end date is uncertain or many lengths are needed.
